content: Methylchloroisothiazolinone, also known as 5-chloro-2-methyl-4-isothiazolin-3-one, is a preservative that exhibits both antibacterial and antifungal properties. It belongs to the chemical group of isothiazolinones. This compound is effective against a wide range of microorganisms, including gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi. It is commonly incorporated into water-based personal care products and cosmetics. Additionally, it is utilized in various industrial applications, such as the production of adhesives, detergents, paints, fuels, and other manufacturing processes. When combined with methylisothiazolinone, it is marketed under the registered trade name Kathon CG. Methylchloroisothiazolinone can also be formulated with alcohols and other long-chain organic compounds, such as methylchloroisothiazolinone ethylparaben benzalkonium chloride or methylchloroisothiazolinone 2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol benzalkonium chloride. Its use in cosmetics dates back to the 1970s. At high concentrations, methylchloroisothiazolinone can cause chemical burns and is known to be an irritant to the skin and mucous membranes. Due to these adverse effects, it has been largely removed from most cosmetic products, except for those designed for short-duration skin contact, such as rinse-off products. In formulations where it is included, its presence is often adjusted to make it more tolerable for individuals with sensitive skin, allowing its use in cosmetic creams and lotions that require direct skin contact. In the United States, the maximum allowable concentrations are 15 parts per million (ppm) for rinse-off products and 8 ppm for other cosmetic applications. Safety Concerns Methylchloroisothiazolinone, like several other common cosmetic ingredients, has been evaluated for its potential carcinogenicity. It is also recognized as an allergen, capable of triggering allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.
